paragraphs: Strategic classification studies decisions where people can change their observable features to obtain a favorable outcome, paying a cost for those changes. This paper examines what happens when people do not know the exact classifier. Instead, they share a prior belief about it and choose changes according to their expected benefit.

The learner can influence these choices by revealing information that is truthful but incomplete. The authors show that partial disclosure can improve classification accuracy: it can allow qualified people to pass while preventing unqualified people from doing so. Information disclosure therefore becomes part of the decision problem, alongside the classifier itself.

Computing an agent’s best response is intractable in general. The paper provides oracle-efficient algorithms for low-dimensional linear classifiers and for another setting with a submodularity condition on modification costs. It also gives positive and negative results for choosing the information to disclose, especially when qualification is represented by a single real number. These results identify both opportunities and computational obstacles.
neurips-2024-bayesian-strategic-classifi.tldr: Truthful but partial disclosure of a classifier can improve accuracy by changing how strategically acting people modify their features.

paragraphs: GovSim is a simulation for studying whether language-model agents can cooperate over a shared resource. Each agent participates in a society that must balance taking resources now with keeping enough available for the future. The setting brings strategic planning, negotiation, and ethical reasoning into the same repeated decision problem.

The authors build an agent architecture and test leading open and closed language models. All but the most powerful agents fail to reach a sustainable equilibrium, and even the highest reported survival rate remains below 54%. Ablation experiments indicate that successful communication between agents is critical to cooperation in these tested cases.

The analysis links many failures to difficulty forming and assessing hypotheses about how present actions affect the group over time. Agents using Universalization-based moral reasoning achieve significantly better sustainability. The contribution is therefore both a testing environment and evidence about mechanisms associated with cooperation. The released environment, prompts, results, and interface support further investigation of sustainable self-government among agents.
neurips-2024-cooperate-or-collapse-emerg.tldr: GovSim exposes widespread failures of sustainable cooperation among tested LLM agents and finds improvements from communication and Universalization-based reasoning.

paragraphs: Scene flow estimation predicts a field of motion vectors from a source point cloud to a target point cloud. For autonomous systems, an accurate motion estimate is valuable, but so is knowing when it may be unreliable. DiffSF addresses both objectives by combining a transformer-based estimator with a denoising diffusion model.

During the forward diffusion process, Gaussian noise is gradually added to the correct motion field. The reverse process learns to recover a prediction from randomly sampled noise, using the two point clouds as conditioning information. This turns motion estimation into a process of progressively reconstructing a plausible field from a noisy starting point.

The authors report stronger robustness than prior approaches and state-of-the-art results on standard scene flow benchmarks. Repeating the reverse process with different initial noise produces multiple motion hypotheses. Those hypotheses enable an uncertainty estimate, which the reported experiments use to detect a majority of inaccurate predictions. The same generative process thus supports both motion prediction and assessment of its reliability.
neurips-2024-diffsf-diffusion-models-for.tldr: DiffSF uses diffusion to improve scene flow predictions and generates multiple hypotheses to identify many unreliable estimates.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning combines labeled and unlabeled examples to reduce the amount of human annotation needed. This paper focuses on an earlier decision: which examples should receive labels in the first place? The authors observe that this choice strongly affects performance, particularly when the annotation budget is extremely small.

Their method, Representative and Diverse Sample Selection, chooses a subset of the unlabeled data for annotation. It uses a modified Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm to minimize a new criterion called alpha-Maximum Mean Discrepancy. The criterion guides selection toward examples that collectively represent the data while also providing diversity, making selection an explicit optimization problem.

The authors demonstrate that minimizing this criterion enhances generalization in low-budget learning. Their experiments report consistent improvements across several popular semi-supervised learning frameworks, as well as better performance than state-of-the-art selection methods from active learning and semi-supervised active learning. The findings show that careful allocation of a small labeling budget can complement improvements in how the resulting labels are used.
neurips-2024-enhancing-semi-supervised-l.tldr: RDSS improves low-budget semi-supervised learning by selecting an annotation subset that is both representative and diverse.

paragraphs: FairMedFM addresses a measurement problem in medical imaging: foundation models may perform differently across patient populations, yet researchers lack consistent infrastructure for evaluating those differences. The paper introduces a benchmark and adaptable codebase for studying fairness alongside performance in automated image classification and segmentation.

The benchmark covers 17 medical imaging datasets with different imaging modalities, dimensionalities, and sensitive attributes. It examines 20 foundation models under several ways of using them, including zero-shot learning, linear probing, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and prompting. This breadth allows fairness to be examined across both model choices and downstream usage choices.

The analysis finds bias, different trade-offs between predictive utility and fairness, and disparities that recur on the same datasets across foundation models. Existing unfairness mitigation methods also show limited effectiveness in the evaluation. These findings indicate that changing the model alone may leave recurring disparities unresolved. The extensible benchmark provides a common basis for investigating those patterns and comparing efforts to address them.
neurips-2024-fairmedfm-fairness-benchmar.tldr: FairMedFM benchmarks medical imaging foundation models and reveals recurring population disparities, varied fairness trade-offs, and limited mitigation effectiveness.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets multiple parties train a language model together without directly sharing their data. The authors argue that existing evaluations rely on artificially assembled datasets that miss important properties of real collaborations. FedLLM-Bench supplies a shared testbed intended to make these evaluations more realistic and easier to compare.

The benchmark includes eight training methods, four training datasets, and six evaluation metrics. Three datasets support federated instruction tuning, while one supports federated preference alignment. Their numbers of clients range from 38 to 747. The data capture differences in language, quality, quantity, instructions, text length, embeddings, and preferences across participants.

These variations matter because collaborative training must accommodate participants whose contributions differ in several ways at once. The authors benchmark existing federated learning methods on all four datasets and report empirical insights, including observations about multilingual collaboration. The contribution is a practical evaluation resource: its datasets and methods provide a common setting for investigating how federated language-model training behaves under varied client data.
neurips-2024-fedllm-bench-realistic-benc.tldr: FedLLM-Bench provides realistic, diverse client datasets and a shared evaluation setup for federated language-model training.

paragraphs: FlexCap describes selected regions of an image while allowing control over how much detail each description contains. Given a box around a region, it can produce text ranging from a short object label to a fuller caption. The central capability is control over information density for a particular part of an image.

The model is trained on captions conditioned on their requested length. To support this training, the authors construct large datasets of region descriptions at different lengths using captioned images from the web. This gives the model training examples that connect the same kind of localized visual input with different levels of verbal detail.

FlexCap shows strong dense-captioning performance on Visual Genome. Its local descriptions can also be passed to a language model to build a visual question answering system, which achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot results on multiple benchmarks. Additional experiments demonstrate uses in image labeling, recognizing object attributes, and visual dialogue. Together, these applications show how adjustable regional descriptions can support broader image-understanding tasks.
neurips-2024-flexcap-describe-anything-i.tldr: FlexCap generates descriptions of selected image regions at controllable lengths and supports tasks including visual question answering.

paragraphs: GO4Align addresses task imbalance in multi-task learning, where several tasks are trained together. Its central proposal is to align optimization across tasks by organizing them into groups. The grouping is adaptive: it responds to relationships among tasks during training, making those relationships part of how the optimization is carried out.

The approach combines two mechanisms within an adaptive group risk minimization strategy. Dynamic group assignment clusters similar tasks using information about their interactions. Risk-guided group indicators then use risk information from previous iterations to exploit consistent task correlations. Together, these mechanisms bring both current task relationships and information from earlier optimization steps into the grouping process.

The authors report superior performance across diverse benchmark experiments while also reporting lower computational costs. This makes the result relevant to both prediction quality and the expense of training multiple tasks together. The paper’s stated contribution is a concrete optimization strategy in which adaptive grouping and risk information work together to address imbalance across tasks.
neurips-2024-go4align-group-optimization.tldr: GO4Align adaptively groups related tasks and uses past risk information to improve multi-task optimization at lower reported computational cost.

paragraphs: When a classifier is uncertain, the structure connecting its possible labels can offer a useful response: make a broader prediction. This paper develops hierarchical selective classification, which lets a model reduce the specificity of its answer as uncertainty increases. The goal is to use class relationships when making predictions in settings sensitive to errors.

The authors formalize hierarchical versions of risk and coverage and introduce curves for examining their relationship. They then develop prediction procedures, called inference rules, that determine how to use the hierarchy. An efficient algorithm provides a high-probability guarantee that a target accuracy constraint is met, giving the approach a stated statistical assurance.

The empirical study examines more than a thousand ImageNet classifiers. It finds that CLIP training, pretraining on ImageNet21k, and knowledge distillation improve hierarchical selective performance. These findings connect training choices to how effectively a model can trade prediction specificity for reliability. The framework makes the breadth of an answer an explicit part of evaluating and controlling classifier behavior.
neurips-2024-hierarchical-selective-clas.tldr: Hierarchical selective classification lets uncertain models give broader answers and includes an algorithm with a high-probability target-accuracy guarantee.

paragraphs: Causal representation learning seeks to recover hidden causal structure from observations. This paper studies interventions that can affect several hidden variables at once, without revealing which variables were changed. It relaxes the single-variable intervention assumption while retaining a linear transformation from the hidden variables to the observed data.

The authors establish identification results for general latent causal models, including parametric and nonparametric models, under stochastic interventions. With sufficiently diverse intervention environments, soft interventions allow identification up to ancestors, leaving ambiguity associated with causal ancestry. Hard interventions can enable perfect identification. These are conditional possibilities, with environmental diversity and intervention type determining the stated guarantee.

The guarantees match the best known results for the more restrictive single-node setting. The paper also supplies algorithms that attain them. A central ingredient connects the intervention problem to score functions of the statistical models for different environments. Those relationships both guide the algorithms and constructively establish why the hidden causal representation can be recovered under the stated conditions.
neurips-2024-linear-causal-representatio.tldr: Under linear observation mappings and sufficiently diverse environments, unknown multi-node interventions can identify latent causal models with guarantees depending on intervention type.

paragraphs: This paper models social network links as arising from a mixture of homophily and social influence. Homophily connects similar participants, while influence provides another mechanism for connections. The proposed Non-Euclidean Mixture Model gives these mechanisms separate geometric representations so that link formation can reflect both within a single model.

Homophily is represented in spherical space to accommodate cycles, and influence is represented in hyperbolic space to accommodate hierarchies. A specially designed projection aligns the two spaces. The authors then incorporate the mixture model into NMM-GNN, a graph variational autoencoder whose encoders, priors, and decoder operate in non-Euclidean geometry.

A space-unification loss helps connect the distinct geometric components during learning. On public datasets, NMM-GNN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for social network generation and classification. These empirical results support the usefulness of representing the two proposed link-formation factors with different geometries. The model connects an account of how social links arise to a unified procedure for learning network embeddings.
neurips-2024-non-euclidean-mixture-model.tldr: NMM-GNN models social links through spherical homophily and hyperbolic influence, improving reported network generation and classification results.

paragraphs: Population dynamics research often asks how a population will evolve. This paper focuses on choosing actions that control that evolution. The authors motivate their approach with the gap between models restricted to particular noise-free dynamics and real population changes that can be complex or adversarial.

They introduce an online-control framework and characterize a class of linear dynamical systems that naturally describe evolving populations. For these systems, they develop an efficient controller based on gradients. Its near-optimal regret bounds compare its accumulated performance with a broad class of linear policies, providing a theoretical measure of how well its decisions compete over time.

The empirical evaluation also considers nonlinear population models, including SIR and replicator dynamics, and finds the proposed algorithm effective there. The distinction matters: the stated theoretical bounds concern the characterized linear systems, while the nonlinear results provide experimental support for broader usefulness. The contribution combines a population-oriented mathematical framework, an efficient control procedure, and evidence that the procedure can work beyond its linear modeling setting.
neurips-2024-online-control-in-populatio.tldr: A gradient-based online controller has near-optimal regret guarantees for linear population systems and promising empirical results on nonlinear dynamics.

paragraphs: Policy Mirror Descent offers a theoretically grounded method for sequential decisions, but applying it directly in reinforcement learning requires action-value functions that are not explicitly available. These functions describe the value of taking actions. The paper addresses this obstacle by learning a world model that can supply the needed estimates.

The world model uses conditional mean embeddings to represent the environment. Tools from operator theory then yield a closed-form expression for the action-value function in terms of that learned model. The expression uses simple matrix operations, providing a concrete computational connection between an environment representation and the quantities required for policy improvement.

Combining these estimators with Policy Mirror Descent produces an algorithm called POWR. The authors prove convergence rates to the global optimum and report preliminary experiments in both finite and infinite state settings that support its effectiveness. The contribution links world-model learning to policy optimization through an explicit value-function calculation, with theoretical convergence analysis and initial empirical evidence.
neurips-2024-operator-world-models-for-r.tldr: POWR uses an operator-based world model to estimate action values for Policy Mirror Descent, with proven convergence rates.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption protects data and model privacy during neural-network inference, but computation is expensive. PrivCirNet reduces this cost by restructuring network weights into block-circulant matrices. This converts general matrix-vector operations into one-dimensional convolutions that are better suited to encrypted computation, linking the network’s structure to the encryption protocol’s efficiency.

The framework customizes the encryption encoding to match that structure, with latency reductions proportional to block size. It also searches for a block-size assignment for each layer using a latency-aware objective and second-order information. Layer fusion provides an additional reduction in inference cost. These components jointly address protocol operations and network design.

On Tiny ImageNet, reported latency reductions relative to Bolt are 5.0 times for ResNet-18 and 1.3 times for ViT at equal accuracy. Accuracy improvements over SpENCNN are 4.1% and 12%, respectively. For MobileNetV2 on ImageNet, the paper reports 1.7 times lower latency than Bolt and 4.2% better accuracy than SpENCNN. These comparisons demonstrate benefits across the evaluated architectures.
neurips-2024-privcirnet-efficient-privat.tldr: PrivCirNet co-designs structured network weights and encryption operations to reduce private-inference latency while preserving or improving reported accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper connects fairness in clustering with proportional representation in multiwinner voting. Both settings involve selecting representatives, expressed as cluster centers in one case and election winners in the other. The authors use this connection to relate several fairness guarantees that had been studied through different mathematical definitions.

They show that any clustering satisfying a particular weak proportionality condition also attains the best known approximations to proportional fairness, individual fairness, and the core. They further establish a two-way relationship: an approximation to proportional fairness is also an approximation to individual fairness, and conversely. These results make one fairness property informative about another.

The paper then examines stronger proportional representation requirements, allowing deviations involving several candidate centers rather than only one. Stronger proportionality notions from voting imply approximations to these stronger clustering guarantees. The contribution is a set of theoretical connections showing how representation conditions can deliver several guarantees simultaneously, including guarantees that account for groups considering multiple alternative centers.
neurips-2024-proportional-fairness-in-cl.tldr: Proportional representation conditions from voting imply multiple clustering fairness guarantees and reveal links between proportional and individual fairness.

paragraphs: Random Function Descent approaches optimization by treating the objective as a random function. The authors propose this framework as a way to explain optimization behavior in machine learning and guide step-size selection. Their starting point is a connection between Bayesian optimization, which reasons about uncertain functions, and classical gradient-based optimization.

Gradient-informed Bayesian optimization has a stated computational complexity of O(n³d³), where n is the number of steps and d is the dimension. The paper uses a stochastic Taylor approximation to recover gradient descent with O(nd) complexity. This approximation makes the random-function perspective computationally viable in high dimensions and yields a specific step-size schedule called Random Function Descent.

The resulting method is scale invariant. The framework also supplies a theoretical basis for familiar practices such as gradient clipping and gradually increasing the learning rate during warmup. Its contribution is therefore both computational and explanatory: it derives a scalable optimization procedure while connecting its step-size behavior to heuristics already used in training.
neurips-2024-random-function-descent-67d.tldr: Random Function Descent derives a scalable, scale-invariant gradient-descent schedule from random-function modeling and helps explain clipping and warmup.

paragraphs: Generating several answers and choosing among them is a common way to reduce unacceptable language-model outputs. This paper studies that strategy through communication theory. It treats the generator as a sender transmitting several descriptions through noisy channels, and the reranker as a receiver choosing the description judged most reliable.

The authors derive conditions under which this process becomes asymptotically error-free, meaning it yields an acceptable answer almost surely in the relevant limit. The analysis allows imperfect rerankers described by Mallows or Zipf-Mandelbrot models and statistically dependent channel distributions. Thus, the stated guarantee does not require perfect ranking or independent descriptions, although it still depends on the derived conditions.

The framework produces reranking laws that the authors validate empirically on two language-model tasks: code generation with DeepSeek-Coder 7B and translation of medical data with TowerInstruct 13B. The contribution explains how redundancy and selection can improve reliability together. It offers a conditional theoretical account of reranking, supported by experiments in two distinct generation settings.
neurips-2024-reranking-laws-for-language.tldr: A communication-theoretic analysis identifies conditions for asymptotically reliable reranking despite imperfect rankers and dependent candidate outputs.

paragraphs: Long robotic manipulation tasks often require a sequence of separately learned skills. Small learning imperfections or disturbances during execution can accumulate as one skill hands control to the next. SCaR addresses this chaining problem by making the relationships within skills and between successive skills explicit targets during training.

The framework applies dual regularization during both skill pretraining and fine-tuning. One aspect strengthens dependencies within each subtask skill, while the other reinforces dependencies between consecutive skills. The purpose is to support smoother transitions and more stable execution across a long task, addressing both the behavior of individual skills and their compatibility in sequence.

The authors evaluate SCaR on simulated IKEA furniture assembly and kitchen organization, with an additional simple real-world tabletop pick-and-place validation. The reported results show higher task success rates than relevant baselines and greater robustness to perturbations. These findings support the value of training for skill connections as well as individual skill performance in the evaluated manipulation settings.
neurips-2024-scar-refining-skill-chainin.tldr: SCaR regularizes both individual skills and their connections to improve success and robustness in long robotic manipulation sequences.

paragraphs: Prediction-powered inference combines a small amount of human-labeled data with a larger amount of automatically labeled data to improve statistical estimates. The automatic labels can be biased. This paper asks how to make that combination more informative by separating the data into groups and using stratified sampling.

The proposed method, StratPPI, provides an algorithm for constructing provably valid confidence intervals for parameters of any dimensionality. The derivation does not impose assumptions on the automatic labeling system or the underlying data distribution. Its key design choices concern how to form strata and how to allocate samples among them.

The authors show theoretically and empirically that appropriate stratification and sample allocation can produce substantially tighter confidence intervals than unstratified approaches. Improvement is especially expected when the automatic evaluator’s performance differs across conditional parts of the target data. The result distinguishes interval validity from precision gains: validity is established broadly, while the size of the improvement depends on useful grouping and allocation choices.
neurips-2024-stratified-prediction-power.tldr: StratPPI uses stratified sampling to obtain valid confidence intervals that can be substantially tighter with appropriate grouping and sample allocation.

paragraphs: In multi-team games, agents must coordinate with teammates while responding to other teams. Team-Nash equilibrium describes outcomes where teams jointly respond optimally to one another. This paper asks whether decentralized agents pursuing their own interests can learn behavior near such an equilibrium, even when teammates do not have identical payoffs.

Team-Fictitious Play combines responses to teammates’ most recent actions with beliefs about other teams. It also includes inertia in action updates to support coordination. For zero-sum potential team games with pairwise team interactions, the authors prove convergence near a Team-Nash equilibrium with a quantifiable error bound. The guarantee is specific to this game setting.

The paper extends the dynamics to multi-team Markov games in both model-based and model-free cases. Its convergence analysis addresses the non-stationarity caused by opponents changing their strategies during learning. Simulations compare Team-FP with smooth fictitious play and multiplicative weights updates, and examine how parameters affect convergence speed. Together, the results provide a learning rule and theoretical support for equilibrium-based predictions about decentralized teams.
neurips-2024-team-fictitious-play-for-re.tldr: Team-Fictitious Play coordinates decentralized agents and reaches a bounded neighborhood of Team-Nash equilibrium in zero-sum potential team games.

paragraphs: A vision-language model’s tendency to mention objects absent from an image changes with the instructions it receives. Averaging across prompts does not resolve the comparison problem when those prompts produce descriptions of different lengths. This paper investigates description length as a factor connecting instructions to measured object hallucination.

The authors find that instructions indirectly affect hallucinations through output length, with longer descriptions showing greater hallucination in their investigation. They fit a curve relating length to hallucination and build LeHaCE around it. The framework compares hallucination at a shared description length, reducing the influence of differing output lengths on model evaluations.

LeHaCE also measures the curve’s slope, capturing how strongly hallucination changes as descriptions become longer. This adds information beyond a hallucination score at one length: it characterizes sensitivity to increasing detail. Experiments show more stable, fair, and comprehensive evaluation than existing methods. The contribution is a way to account explicitly for verbosity when assessing whether models accurately describe image contents.
neurips-2024-toward-a-stable-fair-and-co.tldr: LeHaCE compares object hallucination at matched description lengths and measures how hallucination grows with verbosity.

paragraphs: UltraPixel addresses the difficulty of generating very large images, where arranging meaningful content and synthesizing fine detail both become demanding. It uses a cascade of diffusion processes within one model to generate outputs at multiple resolutions, including 1K, 2K, and 4K, while aiming to keep computation efficient.

The architecture uses semantically rich lower-resolution representations from a later denoising stage to guide high-resolution generation. Implicit neural representations support continuous upsampling, and scale-aware normalization adapts to different resolutions. These components let information about the image’s content guide the construction of a more detailed output across different target sizes.

Both resolution processes operate in a compact space and share most parameters. High-resolution output requires less than 3% additional parameters, which the authors connect to better training and inference efficiency. They report fast training with reduced data requirements, photorealistic high-resolution images, and state-of-the-art performance in extensive experiments. The approach combines reusable semantic structure with resolution-adaptive components to make multi-resolution generation more economical.
neurips-2024-ultrapixel-advancing-ultra-.tldr: UltraPixel shares compact diffusion representations across resolutions to generate detailed images up to 4K with less than 3% additional high-resolution parameters.

paragraphs: Road map construction must recover static geometry such as lane lines and road markings even when moving objects hide them. MapUnveiler uses information across neighboring video frames to address these occlusions. Its basic unit is a clip, allowing the model to relate observations over time when constructing a vectorized high-definition map.

Within each clip, the method connects dense image representations with compact clip tokens to uncover obscured map elements. It propagates those tokens between clips to use longer-term information as well. A temporal stride avoids redundant computation while the pipeline builds relationships across the map, combining temporal context with an efficient processing design.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on nuScenes and Argoverse2. In a challenging evaluation with heavily occluded driving scenes, they report a +10.7% mAP improvement over state-of-the-art approaches. These results support using both within-clip interaction and information propagated between clips. The approach makes temporal evidence central to recovering map geometry that individual observations may only partially reveal.
neurips-2024-unveiling-the-hidden-online.tldr: MapUnveiler combines information within and between video clips to improve road-map construction, particularly under heavy occlusion.

paragraphs: Learning-rate warmup gradually increases the size of training updates before reaching a target rate. Through systematic experiments with SGD and Adam, this paper finds that its dominant benefit comes from moving the network into better-conditioned regions of the loss landscape. There, training can tolerate a larger target learning rate.

The ability to use larger target rates improves final performance and makes hyperparameter tuning more robust in the experiments. The authors also identify different behaviors during warmup: training may begin with progressive sharpening or with sharpness reduction. Which regime occurs depends on initialization and parameterization, helping explain why warmup behavior varies across training setups.

Using these observations, the paper shows how to choose the initial learning rate through the loss catapult mechanism. This can reduce the number of warmup steps and, in some cases, remove the need for warmup entirely. The authors also propose an initialization of Adam’s variance that offers similar benefits. These changes turn the mechanism analysis into concrete ways to adjust training.
neurips-2024-why-warmup-the-learning-rat.tldr: Experiments link warmup’s main benefit to tolerating larger learning rates and motivate initialization choices that can shorten or sometimes eliminate warmup.

paragraphs: WizardArena aims to reduce the manual effort and waiting involved in evaluating and improving instruction-following language models. It simulates chatbot competitions offline using open-source language models. The same arena setup serves two purposes: estimating comparative model rankings and generating battle results that guide further model training.

For evaluation, WizardArena predicts rankings from an offline test set. For training, it runs large-scale simulated battles among strong models on instruction data and uses the results to improve a target model. This process supports supervised fine-tuning as well as subsequent preference-based and reinforcement-learning stages, connecting comparison outcomes directly to post-training.

The experiments show that WizardArena’s rankings closely align with those from an online human arena. Models trained using extensive offline battle data also achieve significant improvements during SFT, DPO, and PPO stages. These findings support the simulated arena as both an evaluation tool and a source of training guidance, with empirical agreement to human rankings in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2024-wizardarena-post-training-l.tldr: WizardArena simulates offline model competitions to predict human-arena rankings and generate feedback that improves language-model post-training.
